chapter: Teschemacher, Pee Wee, Noon and Simeon
title: Where the white Chicago hot style came from
summary: Steiner suggests De Faut and Buster Bailey heard Dodds, Noone and Bechet on the South Side; Chace wonders what produced the white players' distinctive hot quality.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Well, I have a suggestion. Vali spoke of playing with Keppard. It probably was at Lorraine Gardens, and probably they allowed him to play the first set or two until Buster Bailey came over. He was playing on a theater job, I believe, and then played with Keppard later in the evening. But Vali was allowed to sit in until Vali came over. Now this sounds, if this is true, and was two or three years earlier, sounds as if both Buster Bailey and Vali might have been influenced by what was happening on the south side. They might have had the opportunity to hear Dodds, and a little later Noon and Bechet.

Well, that makes us suppose that Vali had no white influences at all at that time. He was listening strictly to the colored bands. And, of course, the great question under discussion is where did the distinctively hot style come from that we identify with the Chicago white clarinet players? It must be something innate. They were nervous or something? Who knows? They were desperate or anxious or something, and they got this particular quality into their playing that the colored players didn't have. Who knows? Perhaps because they played with more ease or more confidence, perhaps the white guys were very young and impressionable and over-anxious.
Well, they talked constantly of having made the tour of the south side, and do you think that it was an overall impression then, rather than a note-for-note imitative desire?
